name: Dark gunmetal
lede: Dark gunmetal is a near-black brown-grey whose Japanese library name, Kurotsurubami, means "black chestnut oak," after a dye bark darkened almost to black, and it appears in one fifth of all the paintings in our archive.

sections.title: Kurotsurubami, a blackened oak dye
sections.body:
The Wikipedia survey "Traditional colors of Japan" lists this color under the romanized name Kurotsurubami, written 黒橡 [1]. 黒 is "black" and 橡 names *tsurubami*, the sawtooth oak whose acorn-cap dye gives the ordinary, lighter *tsurubami-iro*; adding "black" marks the same dye bath taken further, toward near-black [1]. The library separately lists a second close Japanese name for this block of color, Sumi-iro, "ink color," written 墨色 [1]. Neither name is independently dated in the books consulted here [1].

The nearest already-named color in our library is simply [[black]], at a color-distance of 5.4, and the library flags a near-duplicate entry, "Ink," at just 2.0 [1]. The hex, #252321, is a modern screen approximation, not a measurement of dyed cloth or ink [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A color within range of this swatch is the single most common in our archive: it appears in 4,907 of the 23,781 paintings, about 20.6 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it 4,532 times [2]. No other named color in our set reaches a higher share [2].

It peaks in the 1600s, present in 1,545 of 6,394 paintings from that century, 1.2 times the expected rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a shadow, in just over half the paintings that carry it, which fits a near-black tone [2]. Pieter van der Werff is its most devoted painter, using it in 27 of his 35 works here, nearly four times his museums' baseline rate [2]. The earliest dated appearance we have is 1175, and it shares canvases with two colors our data calls Vienna Smoke and Jacaranda Brown more often than chance would predict, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].

openers: Dark gunmetal is the single most common color in our 23,781-painting archive, found in about one painting in five.
Its Japanese name, Kurotsurubami, names a chestnut-oak dye taken all the way to near-black.

issues: No book-level source for the dyeing craft beyond the library gloss; stated as undocumented rather than guessed.
